analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the corporate alternative minimum tax entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations normally compute their taxes two ways and pay the higher amount: the regular tax, or the alternative minimum tax (AMT), a parallel tax designed to ensure profitable corporations pay at least some tax even after using deductions and credits. This bill would abolish the corporate AMT for tax years after 2006, letting corporations pay only the regular tax even if it comes out to zero. The bill was sent to the Ways and Means Committee in March 2007 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations whose deductions and credits currently push them onto the AMT — mostly large, profitable companies — would pay less tax, in some cases nothing, because the bill zeroes out their tentative minimum tax [S3][S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations now paying the corporate AMT

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a sentence to the tax code making the tentative minimum tax zero for every corporation for tax years beginning after December 31, 2006, so no corporation would owe the AMT [S3].
It would spare corporations the cost of computing a second tax system and the AMT liability that comes from claiming deductions, credits, and accelerated depreciation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — meaning taxpayers generally — would absorb the lost revenue, since the AMT exists to collect a floor of tax from profitable corporations whose regular tax has been reduced to zero or near zero by deductions and credits. The bill contains no replacement revenue source [S3].

drawbacks.text: The corporate AMT is the backstop that forces profitable corporations to pay some minimum tax even after deductions and credits wipe out their regular liability; repealing it removes that floor entirely, allowing some profitable corporations to owe nothing [S3].
The bill includes no offsetting revenue, so the corporate tax cut would add to deficits or be paid for through other taxes or spending cuts affecting the public [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows to a narrow set of large corporations with enough deductions and credits to trigger the AMT, while the cost — several billion dollars a year in forgone revenue by general estimates of the corporate AMT — falls on federal taxpayers broadly. There is a fair argument that the AMT is a badly designed tax that penalizes companies for using investment incentives, but this bill repeals it without fixing the underlying system or replacing the revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced in March 2007, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Representative Phil English and 10 other Republicans introduced the Corporate AMT Repeal on March 7, 2007 [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
Sixteen Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers generally are better off, because the corporate AMT — the floor of tax that profitable corporations pay when deductions and credits erase their regular liability — remained in place. The corporations the bill was written for gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, since the corporate AMT survived

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the corporate AMT and recruited 10 original cosponsors [S1][S3].

for.name: 16 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Sam Johnson, Pete Sessions, Geoff Davis, Jim Jordan, and John Doolittle [S4][S3].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it [S5].

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large corporations subject to the AMT
industries.note: Repeal would let corporations whose deductions and credits have erased their regular tax liability pay nothing instead of the AMT floor. Their gain is federal revenue the public otherwise collects [S3].
Corporations and their tax advisers spend resources computing a second tax system; repeal would eliminate that AMT compliance work while shrinking demand for it.
